Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "At Bellweather Bakery, the order form sat on a wooden stand beside the front counter, where customers could fill it out while the morning queue moved past the pastry case. The form had been revised in March after several people asked whether a cake order needed to be placed in person. It now offered three ways to submit a request: customers could hand the paper to a clerk, leave it in the brass box near the entrance, or send a clear photograph of the completed form by email. A small note beneath the contact details explained that the bakery would call if any part of an emailed order was difficult to read.

The first section collected the information needed to identify the customer and the pickup. It asked for a name, a phone number, a preferred contact method, and the requested pickup date and time. A separate line asked whether someone other than the customer would collect the order. The staff had added that question after a few customers arrived at the counter only to learn that a neighbor or relative had been planning to pick up the cake. The form did not require an alternate collector’s phone number, but it provided a blank for one in case the customer wanted to include it.

The cake section began with a choice of size and flavor. Customers could select a round cake for six, ten, or sixteen servings, or request a rectangular cake and specify the number of servings. The flavor list included vanilla, chocolate, lemon, almond, and a rotating seasonal option. The seasonal flavor changed every few weeks, so the form directed customers to ask a clerk what was currently available rather than assume that a flavor mentioned on an older copy would still be offered. Beneath the list, a short field allowed customers to request a combination, such as chocolate cake with lemon filling. The form explained that combinations depended on the bakery’s current ingredients and preparation schedule.

A box labeled “Dietary information” invited customers to describe an allergy or other dietary need. It did not present every request as something the kitchen could accommodate. Instead, the note said, “Please tell us what you need, and we will contact you if we cannot safely prepare it.” The bakery used shared equipment for several products, including those made with nuts, dairy, and wheat. Staff therefore checked the production schedule before promising an adjustment, and the form advised customers not to treat an unconfirmed request as a guarantee. The wording was direct without making the box seem like a special application that most customers should skip.

The next section covered decoration. Customers could choose a border color, describe a general theme, and request a short message for the top of the cake. The message field included a reminder that space was limited, especially on smaller cakes. A customer who wanted a longer inscription could ask whether the bakery could provide a separate card. The form also asked people to identify any image or lettering they planned to bring in themselves. Staff needed to know whether a printed image would be supplied at the counter or sent ahead, because edible printing required a suitable file and a little extra preparation time. The form did not ask customers to submit artwork before confirming that the bakery could print it.

A numbered guide on the back helped customers complete less familiar parts of the form:

1. Choose the cake size, flavor, and filling, if desired.
2. Describe the decoration and write the exact message to be placed on the cake.
3. Add any dietary information, then wait for a staff member to confirm whether the request can be accommodated.
4. Provide a pickup date and time, along with a phone number where the bakery can reach you.

The guide was short enough to read while standing at the counter, but it also clarified that filling in the form did not reserve a pickup time by itself. A clerk checked each request against the day’s schedule and contacted the customer if the requested time was unavailable. For forms left in the brass box, a copy of the pickup details was not automatically returned, so customers were encouraged to write down the date and time they had requested. The bakery’s confirmation call or email supplied the final pickup information.

Price was handled in its own section because the cost could depend on size, filling, decoration, and any special preparation. The form provided a space for the bakery to write an estimate and another space for the customer to note a budget. It did not require a customer to state a budget, and it did not treat one as a fixed price. A staff member could discuss options if the estimate exceeded the amount listed. The form also made clear that the price might change if the customer later requested a different size or additional decoration. Any change was discussed before the bakery updated the order details, rather than being added silently when the cake was collected.

When a paper form reached the counter, the clerk reviewed it with the customer if time allowed. If the counter was busy, the clerk checked the request later and used the preferred contact method to ask about unclear handwriting or missing information. One common question concerned whether “no writing” meant that the cake should have no decoration at all. The staff learned to ask what the customer had in mind rather than infer a full design from that phrase. A blank message line could mean that the customer did not want words on the cake, while the decoration fields still described a border or color. That distinction helped the baker prepare the right cake without making the form longer than necessary.

The bakery kept completed forms in a dated folder behind the counter until pickup. The folder let staff check the cake’s flavor, decoration, and collection time without relying on a note attached to the box. At the end of each week, the manager reviewed forms that had raised questions and marked any wording that customers had misunderstood. That review had led to the new alternate-collector line and the clearer note about seasonal flavors.
